lessons.title: Why the AI Act exists
lessons.subtitle: Why the EU created a single AI law on the CE pattern

sections.title: 27 national AI laws in the pipeline
sections.content:
By 2023 several Member States were drafting AI rules of their own, among them France's CNIL and Spain's AESIA; Italy's Garante banned ChatGPT in March 2023. Without harmonisation a German SME would have served 27 compliance regimes, each with its own definitions, reporting duties and fines.

Recital 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 names the problem: divergent national rules fragment the internal market. The Commission pursues two objectives, trustworthy AI in the internal market and innovation (Article 1(1), points (a) and (h)).

**Legal basis** is Article 114 TFEU (internal market), not Article 16 TFEU (data protection). The AI Act treats AI as a product, and one set of rules applies across all 27 Member States.

sections.title: Why voluntary commitments were not enough
sections.content:
Between 2019 and 2023 voluntary guidance piled up: the OECD AI Principles, the Ethics Guidelines of the EU High-Level Expert Group and many industry codes. None of it stopped large technology companies from rolling out social-scoring prototypes, mass biometric surveillance in public spaces and emotion recognition at work in a legal grey area.

Recital 8 therefore calls for harmonised rules, because voluntary codes do not protect fundamental rights well enough.

**Brussels Effect 2.0:** whoever sells in the EU meets EU rules, and few providers build a separate version for 500 million consumers. That is how the GDPR became the model for California's CCPA, Brazil's LGPD and Japan's APPI.

sections.title: The CE tradition, the Machinery Regulation, and product liability
sections.content:
The AI Act is product-safety law. Through Regulation 765/2008, the New Legislative Framework, it follows the CE logic machinery builders have known for decades: conformity assessment, notified body, technical documentation, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, market surveillance. Makers of CE-marked machinery, medical devices or toys often just add an AI chapter.

**The GDPR applies alongside.** Article 2(7) leaves it unaffected. Whoever feeds personal data into an AI system complies with both. The GDPR governs whether you may process data, the AI Act how the system has to work (Recital 9).

**Directly applicable.** As an EU regulation (Article 288(2) TFEU), the AI Act applies in all 27 Member States without transposition. The prohibitions in Article 5 and the AI-literacy duty in Article 4 have applied directly since 2 February 2025.

quiz.questionText: What is the primary legal basis for the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: Article 114 TFEU, internal-market harmonisation
Article 16 TFEU, data protection
Article 4 TEU, national security
Article 101 TFEU, competition law

quiz.explanation: The AI Act rests on Article 114 TFEU and aims to prevent national fragmentation of the internal market (Recital 3).

quiz.questionText: Why did the EU decide against relying only on voluntary commitments?

answerOptions.text: Voluntary codes had not protected fundamental rights well enough
The GDPR already covers every AI risk
The OECD AI Principles apply only in the US
Voluntary commitments are unlawful in the EU

quiz.explanation: Recital 8 calls for harmonised rules because voluntary codes do not secure enough protection for fundamental rights.

quiz.questionText: Which existing regulation does the AI Act supplement rather than replace?

answerOptions.text: The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679)
The Machinery Directive is replaced in full
CE marking no longer applies to AI products
The Product Liability Directive is repealed

quiz.explanation: Article 2(7) leaves the GDPR unaffected, so both apply side by side.

lessons.title: Roles: provider, deployer, importer, and distributor
lessons.subtitle: Your role sets most of your obligations.

sections.title: The roles in Article 3
sections.content:
Your role under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 sets your obligations:

- **Provider (Article 3(3)):** develops an AI system and places it on the market under its own name or trademark, such as OpenAI, Microsoft, Aleph Alpha, SAP.
- **Deployer (Article 3(4)):** uses an AI system under its own authority in a professional activity, such as any SME with ChatGPT Enterprise, Personio or an AI feature in DATEV.
- **Authorised representative (Article 3(5)):** a person established in the EU with a mandate from a third-country provider.
- **Importer (Article 3(6)):** first places an AI system carrying a third-country trademark on the EU market.
- **Distributor (Article 3(7)):** any other actor in the supply chain besides the provider and the importer.

Most SMEs start as deployers.

sections.title: Where the role flips
sections.content:
**Case 1 (deployer):** A machinery builder uses a startup's predictive-maintenance model unchanged in its plant.

**Case 2 (provider):** The same builder trains the model further on its own sensor data and sells the plant, model included, under its own trademark. That makes it the provider (Article 25), and the further training can also be a substantial modification (Article 3(23)). For a high-risk system it carries the full conformity-assessment duty.

**Case 3 (deployer):** The HR lead uses Personio with AI matching switched on to shortlist applicants. Personio is the provider; the employer is a deployer with extra obligations, because applicant matching is a high-risk use case (Annex III, point 4).

**Case 4 (importer):** An HR consultant sells a US applicant-screening bot through her website to German clients. The US provider has no EU establishment, so she is the importer.

White-label an AI system, modify it substantially or sell it under your own trademark, and you become the provider with all provider obligations (Article 25).

sections.title: Operator or not: the private exemption (Article 2(10))
sections.content:
Article 3(8) groups all four roles, plus authorised representatives and product manufacturers, under the term **operator**. Every operator is bound at least by Article 4 on AI literacy, whatever its precise role.

**The private exemption:** Article 2(10) excludes natural persons who use AI in a purely personal, non-professional activity, such as ChatGPT for their own texts, images or tax return.

- A private individual plans a holiday with ChatGPT: **not caught**.
- The same person, as an employee, writes customer correspondence with ChatGPT: **caught**, because the employer uses it professionally as a deployer (Article 3(4)).
- A managing director drafts quotations with ChatGPT: **caught**, because her company is the deployer.
sections.keyTakeaway: Whoever uses AI purely privately is not a deployer within the meaning of the Regulation (Article 2(10)). Professional use is caught, however small the business.

quiz.questionText: A machinery maker further trains a bought-in predictive-maintenance model and sells the machine with it under its own trademark. What role does it have?

answerOptions.text: Deployer, because it uses the model itself
Provider, because it markets it under its own trademark
Distributor, because it only resells the model
Importer, because the model came from a startup

quiz.explanation: Placing a system on the market under your own trademark makes you the provider (Article 3(3), Article 25); the further training can also be a substantial modification.

quiz.questionText: Who is NOT within the scope of the AI Act?

answerOptions.text: A managing director drafting quotations with ChatGPT
A private individual doing a tax return with ChatGPT
An SME using Personio with AI applicant matching
A freelancer using Copilot for client presentations

quiz.explanation: Article 2(10) excludes purely personal, non-professional use by natural persons; professional use is caught.

quiz.questionText: An SME uses a US provider's AI system unchanged in its own operations. What role does it have?

answerOptions.text: Deployer
Importer
Provider
Distributor

quiz.explanation: Using an AI system under your own authority makes you a deployer (Article 3(4)); the importer is whoever first places it on the EU market (Article 3(6)).

lessons.title: Extraterritorial scope
lessons.subtitle: Why the AI Act covers US providers once their output is used in the EU

sections.title: The output trigger: Article 2(1), point (c)
sections.content:
OpenAI in San Francisco produces a contract summary and a clerk in Nuremberg reads it. That brings OpenAI within the scope of the AI Act.

Article 2(1), point (c), of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 covers providers and deployers established in a third country where the output of the AI system is used in the Union. Recital 22 says this prevents circumvention of the Regulation and protects natural persons located in the Union.

**Consequence:** a US provider has to appoint an EU authorised representative wherever Article 22 requires one, or it may not place the system on the market. Before you sign, ask how the US provider meets its obligations.

sections.title: The authorised representative in the EU
sections.content:
Article 3(5) defines the **authorised representative** as a natural or legal person located or established in the EU with a written mandate to perform a provider's obligations. Article 22 requires third-country providers of the covered high-risk AI systems to appoint one. OpenAI and Microsoft (both Ireland), Salesforce and Workday run EU entities or representation arrangements, Article 22 being one reason.

Three questions belong in the next vendor contract:

- **Who is the EU authorised representative (Article 22)?** Name, registered office, contact details.
- **Does the technical documentation under Article 11 exist?** Then have access on request written into the contract.
- **How is the system classified?** Prohibited practice, high risk under Annex III or Annex I, an Article 50 transparency case, minimal risk, or a general-purpose AI model.

A vendor who cannot answer quickly cannot substantiate its AI Act compliance.

sections.title: Provider and deployer obligations
sections.content:
When your SaaS provider has to implement the AI Act, it handles provider-side transparency under Article 50, the technical documentation and any applicable conformity assessment for its own system.

Your deployer obligations stay with you. For high-risk AI systems Article 26 lists them: follow the provider's instructions for use, ensure human oversight, keep logs where required, and check that input data under your control is relevant and sufficiently representative.

Write provider-compliance clauses into every new SaaS contract and have the declaration of conformity and the authorised representative confirmed in writing.

quiz.questionText: A US SaaS provider with no EU establishment supplies AI output used by an SME in Bavaria. Does the AI Act apply to it?

answerOptions.text: Yes, under the output trigger in Article 2(1), point (c)
No, because it is established outside the EU
Only if it actively markets in the EU
Only if its servers are in the EU

quiz.explanation: Article 2(1), point (c), covers third-country providers once the output is used in the EU, to prevent circumvention.

quiz.questionText: What is the role of an authorised representative under Article 3(5)?

answerOptions.text: They take over all of the provider's obligations
An EU-established person acting for the provider under a written mandate
They must be a German lawyer
They are needed only for general-purpose AI models

quiz.explanation: The representative is established in the EU and acts for the provider under a written mandate without replacing it (Article 3(5), Article 22).

quiz.questionText: What should an SME ask a US AI provider in a vendor assessment?

answerOptions.text: Only the price; the rest is the vendor's business
Authorised representative, technical documentation, risk classification
Only its GDPR privacy notice
Only the server location

quiz.explanation: Without the representative (Article 22), the technical documentation (Article 11) and the classification, you cannot meet your deployer obligations under Article 26.

lessons.title: Timeline: February 2025, August 2025, August 2026, December 2027, August 2028
lessons.subtitle: What applies now and what follows in August 2026, 2027 and 2028

sections.title: The application dates and the amended high-risk timetable
sections.content:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 entered into force on **1 August 2024** and applies in stages:

- **2 February 2025:** Article 4 on AI literacy and most of the prohibitions in Article 5 apply.
- **2 August 2025:** the rules for general-purpose AI models, the governance structure and much of the penalties framework apply; Commission enforcement against providers of general-purpose AI models starts on **2 August 2026**.
- **27 July 2026:** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 enters into force and amends Article 4, individual prohibitions, transitional provisions and the high-risk timetable, among other things.
- **2 August 2026:** the transparency obligations in Article 50 and further general application points apply.
- **2 December 2027:** high-risk rules for stand-alone systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III.
- **2 August 2028:** high-risk rules for product-embedded systems under Article 6(1) and Annex I.

The high-risk dates are applicable law under the published amending regulation. Systems placed on the market before the new dates have transitional rules of their own.

sections.title: Your tasks per deadline
sections.content:
Article 4 prescribes no particular form of documentation and, since the amendment, no guaranteed individual level of competence (as of 28 July 2026). Providers and deployers must take measures that support the development of AI literacy in a way that fits the context.

**Now:**

- an inventory of every AI system in the house, shadow IT included
- a risk classification per system (Annex III, Article 5, general-purpose AI or low risk)
- documented Article 4 measures that fit the role and the risk
- the notices under Article 50 in place by 2 August 2026, wherever the conditions are met

**For 2027 and 2028:**

- plan high-risk systems: stand-alone ones for **2 December 2027**, product-embedded ones for **2 August 2028**
- prepare vendor documents, logs, human oversight and, where required, a fundamental rights impact assessment

A substantial modification can end transitional treatment or trigger a fresh assessment, so classify again after every major update.

sections.title: When does enforcement begin?
sections.content:
Article 99 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 tiers fines in three levels. For undertakings the higher of the two figures applies:

- **Prohibited practices (Article 5):** up to **EUR 35 million or 7%** of total worldwide annual turnover (Article 99(3))
- **Obligations listed in Article 99(4):** up to **EUR 15 million or 3%**
- **Incorrect information to authorities:** up to **EUR 7.5 million or 1%** (Article 99(5))

SMEs, and since the amendment small mid-caps, have upper limits of their own. The calculation and the penalty tier depend on the case, the provision infringed, its application date and the competent authority.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 4 has applied since February 2025, in amended form since 27 July 2026. National supervision and enforcement begin in early August 2026, according to the Commission FAQ.

quiz.questionText: Since when has the AI-literacy duty under Article 4 applied?

answerOptions.text: 2 August 2026
2 February 2025
2 August 2027
1 August 2024

quiz.explanation: Under Article 113, point (a), Chapter I, including Article 4, applies from 2 February 2025. According to the Commission FAQ, national supervision starts on 2 August 2026.

quiz.questionText: Which date did Parliament and the Council adopt for stand-alone high-risk systems under Annex III?

answerOptions.text: 2 August 2025
2 August 2026
2 August 2027
2 December 2027

quiz.explanation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, sets 2 December 2027 for stand-alone Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for product-embedded Annex I systems.

quiz.questionText: What is the maximum fine for an infringement of the prohibitions in Article 5?

answerOptions.text: EUR 7.5 million or 1% of turnover
EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover
EUR 35 million or 7% of turnover, whichever is higher
EUR 50 million or 10% of turnover

quiz.explanation: Article 99(3) provides for up to EUR 35 million or 7%; for SMEs, Article 99(6) applies the lower amount.
